name: bluewater-17-the-man-who-never-called-back
lines: All rise. Court is now in session.
The case. The people, versus a man who never called anyone back.
Meet the defendant. Dale. He's made up. You know a Dale. You might be a Dale.
He's a good electrician. Nobody disputes that. That's what makes this a tragedy.
The charge. Forty one missed calls, in a single month. He pleads, busy.
The first witness.
The prosecution calls a homeowner. Her kitchen lights went out on a Monday.
She called Dale at nine. It rang, and rang, and went to a voicemail that said, mailbox full.
Did you leave a message? I could not, she says. The mailbox was full.
Since when? The court checked. Since twenty twenty two.
So what did you do? She shrugs. I called the next guy. He picked up.
Gasps in the courtroom.
Exhibit A.
The prosecution presents Dale's own phone.
Forty one missed calls. Nineteen voicemails he never heard. And one text, from his mother. Call me back.
He didn't.
Objection, says Dale. I was on a ladder. Sustained. Everyone's on a ladder, Dale.
The question isn't why you missed the call. It's what happened in the next ten minutes.
And in Dale's case, what happened was, nothing. For six days.
The defense.
Dale takes the stand. He's sweating.
My work speaks for itself, he says.
The judge leans in. Does it, Dale? Because it can't seem to answer the phone.
I get all my jobs from word of mouth.
And when the mouth says, call Dale, and nobody answers, what does the mouth say next?
Silence.
It says, don't bother with Dale.
The surprise witness.
The prosecution calls its final witness. The courtroom doors open.
It's the next guy.
He's not better than Dale. He says so himself. I'm actually worse at wiring.
So how did you get the lights job? And the panel upgrade after it? And her sister's whole basement?
He holds up his phone. I answered it.
That's it? That's it. Sometimes I just text, on a job, call you at noon. Then I call at noon.
Dale stares at the floor. Three jobs. One customer. Gone to a man who is, quote, worse at wiring.
The verdict.
Guilty. On all forty one counts.
But the judge isn't done. Dale, you're not a bad electrician. You're a great one, that nobody can reach.
So here's your sentence. Four things. Starting tonight.
One. Empty the mailbox. Record a new greeting. Your name, your business, and when you call back.
Two. Miss a call, send a text. On a job, I'll call you by noon. It takes eight seconds.
Three. Then actually call at noon. That's the entire trick.
Four. If you truly can't keep up, somebody else answers. A person, a service, anybody but a full mailbox.
Dale raises his hand. What if they just want a price? Then give them a range, Dale. A range is not a crime.
The court will be honest. Answering the phone won't fix a business by itself.
And nobody can promise how many of those calls turn into jobs.
But a call you never return is the one job you are guaranteed to lose.
One month later.
Dale's phone rings. He's on a ladder.
He lets it ring. Fine. Then he climbs down, and types eight seconds of text.
On a job. Call you at noon.
At noon, he calls.
The woman on the other end says, oh. You called back.
Case closed.
You don't need to be the best in town. You need to be the one who calls back.
Court is adjourned. And call your mother.
If your marketing needs somebody on the case, that's us. Bluewater Co dot C A.
